topics.title: Starting a Conversation
topics.short: Open with a greeting and a simple question or comment about something you share, like the class, the game or the food.
topics.trouble: Learners wait for the other person to start, or open with a fact about themselves. A friendly question about the moment you share is the easiest door.

topics.title: Asking Good Questions
topics.short: Open questions ("What was the best part of your trip?") keep a conversation going; yes-or-no questions often stop it.
topics.trouble: Learners ask a string of yes-or-no questions and then run out of things to say. Questions that begin with what, how and why invite a real answer.

topics.title: Listening Well
topics.short: Good listeners look at the speaker, let them finish, and ask a follow-up question about what they just said.
topics.trouble: Learners spend the other person's turn planning their own story. A follow-up question proves you heard, and it is the best way to keep talking.

topics.title: Sharing the Conversation
topics.short: A conversation is a game of catch: say a little, then toss it back with a question, and bring quiet people in.
topics.trouble: Learners answer one question with a long story and never ask one back, or keep steering every topic to themselves.

topics.title: Topics to Skip
topics.short: Remarks about someone's body, weight, money or a private family matter make people uncomfortable; leave those out.
topics.trouble: Learners think a remark is fine because it is true or meant kindly, like "You got so tall!" or "Your house is small." If it is about someone's body or money, skip it.

topics.title: Ending a Conversation Politely
topics.short: End with a kind closing line, like "It was good to talk with you; I need to find my mom," and a goodbye.
topics.trouble: Learners walk away in the middle of a sentence or stay stuck because leaving feels rude. A friendly closing line ends things well for both people.

topics.title: Introducing Yourself
topics.short: Stand, smile, look at the person, say "Hi, I'm Leo," and add one detail that gives them something to talk about.
topics.trouble: Learners mumble their name while looking down, so it has to be asked again. Say it clearly, then add a detail: "I'm Sam's cousin."

topics.title: Eye Contact
topics.short: In the U.S., looking at someone's face while you greet and listen shows interest and respect; in some cultures, less direct eye contact is the respectful way.
topics.trouble: Learners stare without blinking or never look up. Look at the face, glance away now and then, and know that other families and cultures may do it differently.

topics.title: A Good Handshake
topics.short: Stand, reach out your right hand, meet palm to palm, grip firmly but not hard, shake two or three times, and let go.
topics.trouble: Learners give a limp "fingertip" shake or a crushing squeeze, or stay seated. A firm grip and a smile while standing is the custom.

topics.title: Remembering and Using Names
topics.short: Repeat a new name right away ("Nice to meet you, Grace"), use it once more, and ask again soon if you missed it.
topics.trouble: Learners are too embarrassed to ask for a name again, so they avoid using it for weeks. Asking again right away is easy and polite.

topics.title: Introducing Two People
topics.short: Say the name of the older or honored person first, then present the other person to them, and give each a detail to talk about.
topics.trouble: Learners say the names in any order, or say only the names and walk off. "Grandma, this is my friend Omar. Omar, this is my grandmother, Mrs. Hale. Omar plays chess too."

topics.title: Addressing Adults
topics.short: Use Mr., Ms., Mrs. or Dr. with a last name unless an adult invites you to use a first name; sir and ma'am are customary in many regions.
topics.trouble: Learners guess wrong between Mrs. and Ms. "Ms." works for any woman when you are not sure. Customs differ by region and family, so follow what an adult asks to be called.

topics.title: Standing with Poise
topics.short: Stand tall and easy: weight on both feet, shoulders relaxed and back, head up, hands still at your sides.
topics.trouble: Learners stand stiff like a soldier, or slump with hands in their pockets. Poise looks easy and relaxed, not rigid.

topics.title: Sitting Well
topics.short: Sit back in the chair, upright and relaxed, with feet on the floor and hands in your lap or on the table edge.
topics.trouble: Learners sprawl, hang an arm over the chair back, or tip the chair. Sitting well shows you are paying attention to the people with you.

topics.title: Walking into a Room
topics.short: Walk in at an easy pace, look up, smile, greet the people there, and wait to be shown where to sit if you are a guest.
topics.trouble: Learners slip in looking at their phone, or head straight for a seat. A greeting at the door is the polite way to arrive.

topics.title: Standing to Greet
topics.short: Stand up when an adult or a guest enters the room or comes to meet you, and when you are introduced.
topics.trouble: Learners stay seated and wave from the couch. Standing says "you matter enough for me to get up."

topics.title: Setting the Table
topics.short: Fork on the left, knife on the right with the blade toward the plate, spoon to the right of the knife, glass above the knife, napkin on the left.
topics.trouble: Learners put the fork and knife on the same side, or face the blade outward. Forks and "left" both have four letters; knife, spoon and "right" have five.

topics.title: Holding the Fork and Knife
topics.short: In the American style, cut with the fork in the left hand and the knife in the right, then set the knife down and switch the fork to eat; the Continental style keeps the fork in the left hand.
topics.trouble: Learners hold the knife like a dagger or cut a whole plate of food at once. Cut one or two bites at a time; both styles are correct.

topics.title: Passing Food
topics.short: Pass dishes to the right (counterclockwise), offer them to your neighbor first if you are starting, and pass the salt and pepper together.
topics.trouble: Learners take a dish that was passed to someone else, or send the salt without the pepper. The salt and pepper travel as a pair.

topics.title: Serving Yourself
topics.short: Use the serving spoon, not your own fork, take a fair share so there is enough for everyone, and put the spoon back in the dish.
topics.trouble: Learners take a huge first helping of a favorite dish before everyone has some. Count the people and take a fair share; seconds can come later.

topics.title: Reaching and Elbows
topics.short: Ask for what is out of reach, keep elbows off the table while eating, and keep phones, toys and hats away from the table.
topics.trouble: Learners think elbows are never allowed. Most etiquette writers say elbows are fine between courses or after the meal, just not while you are eating.

topics.title: Dropped Forks and Other Mishaps
topics.short: At home, pick up a dropped fork and get a clean one; at a restaurant, leave it and quietly ask for another; wipe a small spill and say "excuse me."
topics.trouble: Learners make a big fuss, or wipe a dropped fork on a napkin and keep using it. Quiet and quick is the rule for any mishap.

topics.title: Thanking the Cook
topics.short: Say something kind about the meal and thank whoever cooked it, and offer to help clear the table.
topics.trouble: Learners thank the cook only when they liked the food. Thank them for the work: "Thank you for dinner. The bread was great."

topics.title: Making a Phone Call
topics.short: Greet the person, say who you are, ask if it is a good time, say why you are calling, and say goodbye before you hang up.
topics.trouble: Learners start talking without saying their name, or call during dinner or late at night. "Hi, this is Ruby, Hana's friend. Is Hana there, please?"

topics.title: Answering and Taking a Message
topics.short: Answer with a greeting, ask "May I tell them who's calling?", and write down the name, number and message.
topics.trouble: Learners shout across the house or forget to write the message down. A message is only helpful if it reaches the person.

topics.title: Video Calls
topics.short: On a video call, find a quiet spot with light on your face, look at the camera, mute when you are not talking, and give the call your attention.
topics.trouble: Learners leave the microphone on while they eat, or walk around with the camera bouncing. Treat a video call like sitting across a table.

topics.title: Texting Courtesy
topics.short: Text at reasonable hours, write clearly, read your message before you send it, and remember tone is hard to hear in text.
topics.trouble: Learners send a curt "k" that reads as annoyed, or text late at night. A short friendly word or two prevents a lot of hurt feelings.

topics.title: Group Chats
topics.short: In a group chat, stay on topic, don't share screenshots or private messages without asking, and never use the chat to leave someone out or gang up.
topics.trouble: Learners think a screenshot is harmless because the words were already sent. Sharing someone's message with others breaks their trust.

topics.title: Phones Around People
topics.short: When someone is talking with you, put the phone down; at meals, visits and conversations, the people in front of you come first.
topics.trouble: Learners text "under the table" and think no one notices. Everyone notices; it tells them they are less interesting than the screen.

topics.title: Having a Friend Over
topics.short: As a host, greet your friend and their parent, offer a snack and a choice of what to do, and include everyone who is there.
topics.trouble: Learners play a game only they enjoy, or leave a sibling or second friend out. The guest's good time is the host's job.

topics.title: Sleepovers
topics.short: At a sleepover, follow the family's rules and bedtime, offer to help, keep things tidy, and thank the parents in the morning.
topics.trouble: Learners stay up after the parents asked for quiet or snack without asking. It is fine to call home if you feel uncomfortable or want to leave.

topics.title: Birthday Party Invitations
topics.short: Reply to an invitation by the date it asks, and don't hand out invitations or talk about a party in front of people who were not invited.
topics.trouble: Learners never reply, or reply and then don't show up. The host needs to know how many are coming; "RSVP" means please reply.

topics.title: Giving a Gift
topics.short: Choose a gift with the person in mind, take the price tag off, add a card with your name, and let them open it when they like.
topics.trouble: Learners choose the gift they would want, or say how much it cost. The thought about the other person is what makes a gift.

topics.title: Receiving a Gift Graciously
topics.short: Read the card first, look at the giver, thank them warmly, and say something kind, even if you already have one or it is not your style.
topics.trouble: Learners say "I already have this" or "Do you have the receipt?" in front of the giver. Thank them for thinking of you; questions about returns come later, privately, if at all.

topics.title: Writing a Thank-You Note
topics.short: A thank-you note has a greeting, a thank-you for the specific gift or kindness, a line about how you will use or enjoy it, a warm closing and your signature.
topics.trouble: Learners write "Thanks for the gift" without naming it, or wait months. Name the gift, add one real detail, and send it within a week or two.

topics.title: Apologizing Well
topics.short: A good apology says what you did, says you are sorry without a "but," offers to make it right, and does better next time.
topics.trouble: Learners say "I'm sorry you feel that way" or "Sorry, but you started it." Those blame the other person. Own your part.

topics.title: Disagreeing Kindly
topics.short: Disagree with the idea, not the person: listen first, say what you agree with, and say your view with "I think" instead of "You're wrong."
topics.trouble: Learners think disagreeing is rude, or that winning the argument is the goal. You can disagree and still be friends.

topics.title: Sportsmanship
topics.short: Play fair, follow the referee's calls, cheer for your team without jeering the other one, and shake hands after the game, win or lose.
topics.trouble: Learners argue every call or celebrate by mocking the other team. A good sport is gracious in both winning and losing.

topics.title: At School and with Teachers
topics.short: Greet your teacher, raise your hand and wait, listen when others speak, and ask for help respectfully.
topics.trouble: Learners call out answers or argue a grade in front of the class. Ask to talk after class instead.

topics.title: Respect for Elders
topics.short: Offer older people your seat, your help with doors and bags, and your attention; listen to their stories and stand when they enter.
topics.trouble: Learners think respect means staying silent. Asking an older relative about their life is one of the kindest things you can do.

topics.title: Helping at Home
topics.short: Do your share of chores without being asked twice, notice what needs doing, and thank family members for what they do.
topics.trouble: Learners help only when it is "their" chore. Family manners are the ones we practice most, with the people we see every day.

topics.title: Lines and Crowds
topics.short: Join a line at the end, leave a little space, keep your bag close, and don't save places for friends who arrive later.
topics.trouble: Learners think saving spots for friends is fine. Each person who joins in front of you makes everyone behind you wait longer.

topics.title: Doors and Elevators
topics.short: Hold a door for the person behind you, let people off an elevator before you get on, and press the button for others.
topics.trouble: Learners rush into an elevator as the doors open. Step aside and let people out first.

topics.title: Sidewalks and Shared Spaces
topics.short: Walk on the right, don't spread out across the whole path in a group, step aside to stop or check your phone, and clean up after yourself.
topics.trouble: Learners stop in the middle of a busy walkway or doorway. If you need to stop, step to the side.

topics.title: At the Movies and Shows
topics.short: Arrive on time, silence your phone and keep the screen dark, save talking for afterward, and clap at the right moments.
topics.trouble: Learners whisper through a movie or check their phone, whose light bothers the people behind them.

topics.title: The Pledge and the National Anthem
topics.short: Under the U.S. Code, during the Pledge and the anthem people stand, face the flag, place the right hand over the heart, and take off hats other than religious head coverings (people in uniform salute).
topics.trouble: Learners keep a hat on or keep talking during the anthem. When no flag is displayed, people face the music. The Code describes customs; it does not punish anyone for not following them.

topics.title: Displaying the Flag
topics.short: On a wall, horizontal or vertical, the flag's blue union goes at the top and to the flag's own right, which is the viewer's left.
topics.trouble: Learners hang a vertical flag with the union at the top right, as seen from the front. Whichever way it hangs, the union is at the top left as you look at it.

topics.title: Respect and Care for the Flag
topics.short: The Flag Code asks that the flag not touch the ground, fly from sunrise to sunset unless lit at night, and be retired in a dignified way when worn.
topics.trouble: Learners think a flag that touches the ground must be destroyed. The Code asks only that it be kept from touching the ground; a clean, undamaged flag can still be flown.
